sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Uncured epoxy systems can irritate skin and cause sensitization; hardeners have their own hazards. Large masses of mixed resin can self-heat rapidly during cure and ignite nearby combustible material.

sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Chemical recycling has been demonstrated for cured cyanate-ester networks. Dreyer and coworkers decomposed bisphenol-A, bisphenol-E and novolac polycyanurates with reactive liquid agents, producing phenolic and triazine-containing material. Resin composition, agent and temperature strongly affected dissolution; this is controlled chemical treatment, not environmental degradation. The recovered hydroxyl-containing mixture was incorporated into new polyurethane foams and solid thermosets. Tests on reinforcement fibers found comparatively small effects on carbon and glass fibers, while aramid and flax compatibility depended on the treatment. The study establishes laboratory recovery and reuse options rather than a universal process for every cyanate-ester composite.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Huntsman’s AROCY L 10 safety sheet describes a bisphenol-E dicyanate precursor that is harmful if inhaled or swallowed and can seriously damage eyes. It also warns of organ effects after repeated exposure and aquatic toxicity. Control vapor or mist, protect against splashes and contain spills. These precursor hazards must be distinguished from those of a cured polycyanurate composite.

sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Used HNBR vulcanizate can be mechanically reduced to powder and incorporated into fresh HNBR compounds. A laboratory study froze and roll-ground the scrap, then modified its surface with 5 wt% trans-polyoctenamer before compounding it into HNBR-4307 hose-lining formulations. The modified powder performed better than unmodified powder at the same loading, although increasing powder content generally reduced tensile and tear properties and increased compression set. This route retains crosslinked particles in a new peroxide-cured rubber matrix; it does not recover HNBR monomer or establish unrestricted replacement of virgin rubber.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Freshly molded HNBR rubber articles can remain an exposure source while cooling. HSE recommends extraction at cooling racks, avoiding skin contamination, and gloves suitable for chemical and heat exposure. These are process controls for formulated rubber articles; the cure package and other ingredients determine additional chemical hazards.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber articles, trimming and finishing are distinct exposure-generating operations. HSE recommends local extraction for finishing emissions, appropriate protection against skin contamination and cleaning without dispersing dust. These controls address fabricated rubber compounds; any additional chemical hazards must be assessed from the grade’s curatives, fillers and processing conditions.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory chlorine reclamation has been demonstrated using commercial polyepichlorohydrin (PECH; reported Mw about 700,000). Liu and colleagues reacted this polymer with 7,8-benzoquinoline using Cu/Pd catalysts and sodium nitrate in DMSO under 3 bar oxygen at 140 °C for 15 h, producing 10-chlorobenzoquinoline. This chemical-reclamation route transfers chlorine into a new product; it does not recover intact rubber or epichlorohydrin monomer. The study used purchased pure polymer, so its result does not establish recovery of compounded, vulcanized CO service parts or commercial operation.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: During polyurethane manufacture or application, unreacted isocyanate ingredients can irritate skin, eyes and airways and cause sensitization or occupational asthma. NIOSH emphasizes enclosure and ventilation to control vapor or aerosol exposure and protection against skin contact. These ingredient hazards concern reactive formulations and cannot be assigned unchanged to a fully cured article.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: WACKER’s silicone-elastomer processing guidance identifies flammable low-molecular siloxanes, and sometimes peroxide by-products, in post-cure emissions. A circulating-air oven needs fresh-air supply and effective exhaust to prevent vapor accumulation. Post-cure conditions and contamination control depend on the formulation; the safety of a cured article is not established solely by calling it silicone.

sources.citation: Wacker Chemie AG, Solid and Liquid Silicone Rubber: Material and Processing Guidelines, document 6709 en/08.25 (2025).
sources.locator: Section 6.1, pages 66–67: volatile low-molecular siloxanes, peroxide by-products and ventilated post-curing; ELASTOSIL silicone rubbers.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A styrenic-block-copolymer handling example is Kraton SIS: its supplier highlights static-charge accumulation, hot-melt burns and exposure to dust or process fumes. Packaging discharge near flammable vapor requires ignition control, and melt handling needs thermal protection. These are documented SIS-grade precautions; the complete compounded product may introduce different additives or solvents.

sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Fluoroelastomer handling depends on material form and formulation. Chemours advises avoiding skin contact with Viton A-201C, which includes cure chemicals. For cured Gumlast perfluoroelastomer parts, the supplier emphasizes hazardous fumes from overheating or burning, including hydrogen fluoride. Thus uncured-compound exposure and severe-heat decomposition need separate controls; ordinary sealing performance does not establish a family-wide safety classification.
